text: Passive dynamic walkers, first designed by Tore McGeer (1990), illustrate morphological computation because they:
choices: Use powerful actuators to control every joint with high precision
Require a detailed internal model of the terrain before each step
Walk with a stable, natural-looking gait down a slight slope using no actuators or control signals at all
Can only walk while tethered to a digital controller
explanation: On a gentle downhill slope, a well-designed passive dynamic walker produces a natural bipedal gait purely through gravity, inertia, and contact forces, with no actuators or control. The lesson is that much of what we take to be a neural computation (walking) is actually 'computed' by body physics; neural systems handle only corrections and energy input. The other options describe exactly the control-heavy approach passive walkers dispense with.
